newsitem.title: ARGENTINA: Insects could take shine off Argentine maize crop.
newsitem.headline: Insects could take shine off Argentine maize crop.

text.p: Argentina's steamy summer is not only proving benign for the crops but has also provoked a population explosion of insects which could threaten the maize crop, analysts and agronomists said Tuesday.

While residents of Buenos Aires are being tortured by stinging clouds of mosquitos, maize fields in many parts of the country are seeing outbreaks -- although still minor -- of the insect-borne "Rio Cuarto disease".

"In my view nothing is definite about the volume of the corn crop in Argentina," said one analyst, who requested anonymity, "It is hard to believe the crop will be small, but its full potential may not be reached."
He said he had heard of Rio Cuarto outbreaks in many parts of the maize belt far from its traditional focus in southern Cordoba and even as distant as Necochea in the south east.
But the analyst stressed that it was still not clear how much effect the disease would have on the crop.
"It's still too early to say. In the same field you find plants in very good condition and others affected," he said.
Rio Cuarto is spread by an insect which drinks the sap from the maize plants and infects them with a disease which stunts its growth.

Food Under Secretary Felix Cirio said last week that the government had taken the disease into account when it announced its estimate for maize output, which at 14.6 million tonnes would be up from 10.5 million tonnes in 1995/96.

Pablo Vernengo, of the Argentine Agronomists Association, said that there had still been no reports of serious Rio Cuarto outbreaks, but that the disease could affect the crop if there was much more wet, warm weather.
"It is still not alarming, but we have to keep an eye on this," he said, "If the humid conditions continue we will have to be alert," he told Reuters.

The government's Meteorological Service forecast warm, mainly dry weather Tuesday, but with a possibility of storms in many parts of the grain belt Wednesday. Weather Services Corp said highs would range from 82-95 (Farenheit, or 28-35 Celsius), on Tuesday.
Rio Cuarto disease usually lurks only in southern Cordoba, but has spread due to the widespread adoption of zero tillage and also the unusually wet summer.
Farmers in other areas unfamiliar with the problem also failed to sow resistant mazie varieties, the analyst said.
But, while overfriendly to insects, the climate has otherwise been very kind to the maize, soybean and sunflower seed crops, which should also benefit from increased fertilizer use.

The analyst said the soybeans are generally in good condition, although some plants could do with a bit more water after a string of hot days with highs around 90 F (32 C). Rain has tended to fall this summer in thunderstorms, sometimes missing certain areas, and not as part of big fronts covering whole swathes of cropland.
"The critical month for soybeans will start in a week's time," the analyst said, "That's when they start defining the quantity of pods and they start to fill out."
He said that while the soybeans would benefit from more rain, this could reduce sunflower yields.
The government's Agriculture Secretariat last week said it expected soybean output of 13.7 million tonnes, wheat output of 15.2 million tonnes and sunflower seed output of 5.6 million tonnes.
